response.text:
In Which the Reader Is Introduced to a Man of Humanity

Late in a chilly February afternoon, two gentlemen sat over their wine in a well-furnished dining-parlor, in the town of P——, Kentucky. No servants were present; the talk was earnest.

For convenience’ sake we say two gentlemen; yet, critically examined, one scarce came under the species. Short and thick-set, gaudily over-dressed in many-colored vest and blue neckerchief bedropped with yellow, hands coarse and ring-laden, a heavy chain with seals jingling,—his swaggering pretension bespoke a low man elbowing upward. His discourse defied Murray’s Grammar, and was garnished with profane expletives which we decline to transcribe. His companion, Mr. Shelby, had the air of a gentleman; house and housekeeping bespoke easy, even opulent circumstances.

“That is the way I should arrange the matter,” said Mr. Shelby.

“I can’t make trade that way—I positively can’t, Mr. Shelby,” returned the other, holding a glass to the light.

“Why, the fact is, Haley, Tom is an uncommon fellow; steady, honest, capable,—manages my whole farm like a clock.”

“You mean honest, as niggers go,” said Haley, helping himself to brandy.

“No; I mean, really, Tom is a good, steady, sensible, pious fellow. He got religion at a camp-meeting, four years ago; and I believe he really did get it. I’ve trusted him, since then, with everything I have,—money, house, horses,—let him go round the country; and I always found him true and square. Last fall, I let him go to Cincinnati alone, to bring home five hundred dollars. ‘Tom,’ says I, ‘I trust you, because I think you’re a Christian.’ Tom comes back, sure enough; some low fellows asked him why he didn’t make tracks for Canada. ‘Ah, master trusted me, and I couldn’t.’”

“Some folks don’t believe there is pious niggers, Shelby,” said Haley, with a candid flourish; “but I do. I had a fellow, now, in this yer last lot I took to Orleans—’t was as good as a meetin’ to hear that critter pray; quite gentle and quiet like. He fetched me a good sum. Yes, I consider religion a valeyable thing in a nigger, when it’s the genuine article.”

“I am sorry to part with Tom. You ought to let him cover the whole balance; and you would, Haley, if you had any conscience.”

“Well, I’ve got just as much conscience as any man in business can afford to keep,—just a little, you know, to swear by, as ’t were,” said the trader jocularly. “I’m ready to do anything in reason to ’blige friends; but this yer is a leetle too hard.”

“Well, then, how will you trade?” said Mr. Shelby.

“Wa’al—haven’t you a boy or gal you could throw in with Tom?”

“Hum!—none I could spare. To tell the truth, it’s only hard necessity makes me willing to sell at all.”

Here the door opened, and a small quadroon boy, between four and five, entered. His floss-silk hair curled glossy about a dimpled face; large dark eyes, full of fire and softness, looked from under long lashes; a scarlet and yellow plaid robe set off his beauty; and a comic assurance, blended with bashfulness, bespoke a petted favorite.

“Hulloa, Jim Crow!” said Mr. Shelby, whistling, and snapping raisins. “Pick that up, now!” The child scampered, and was caressed. “Now, Jim, show this gentleman how you can dance and sing.” He struck up one of those wild, grotesque songs common among the negroes, his whole little body keeping time. “Bravo!” cried Haley, tossing him a quarter of an orange. “Now, Jim, walk like old Uncle Cudjoe, when he has the rheumatism.” Instantly the flexible limbs humped and hobbled; the childish face puckered dolefully; the stick thumped. “Show us how old Elder Robbins leads the psalm.” The boy drew his chubby face to formidable length, and toned through his nose with imperturbable gravity.

“Hurrah! what a young ’un!” said Haley. Clapping Mr. Shelby’s shoulder, he added, “Fling in that chap, and I’ll settle the business—I will.”

At this moment a young quadroon woman, apparently about twenty-five, entered. One glance from the child to her sufficed to mark the mother,—the same rich, full, dark eye and ripples of silky hair; a delicate hand and trim ankle not lost on the trader’s quick appraisement.

“Well, Eliza?” said her master.

“I was looking for Harry, please, sir;” and the boy bounded to show his spoils. “Well, take him away, then,” said Mr. Shelby; and hastily she withdrew with the child.

“By Jupiter,” said the trader, turning in admiration, “there’s an article, now! You might make your fortune on that ar gal in Orleans, any day.”

“I don’t want to make my fortune on her,” said Mr. Shelby, dryly; and, seeking to turn the talk, he praised the wine.

“Capital—first chop!” said the trader; then, slapping Shelby’s shoulder, “Come, how will you trade about the gal?—what’ll you take?”

“Mr. Haley, she is not to be sold,” said Shelby. “My wife would not part with her for her weight in gold.”

“Ay, ay! women always say such things; they ha’nt no calculation. Show ’em how many watches and trinkets one’s weight in gold would buy, and that alters the case, I reckon.”

“I say no, and I mean no,” said Shelby, decidedly.

“Well, you’ll let me have the boy, though; I’ve come down pretty handsome for him.”

“What on earth can you want with the child?” said Shelby.

“Why, I’ve got a friend going into this yer branch—handsome boys to raise for the market. Fancy articles—sell for waiters, and so on, to rich ’uns. It sets off a great place—a real handsome boy to open door, wait, and tend. This little devil is such a comical, musical concern, he’s just the article.”

“I would rather not sell him,” said Mr. Shelby, thoughtfully; “the fact is, sir, I’m a humane man, and I hate to take the boy from his mother.”

“O, you do?—La! yes—something of that ar natur. It’s mighty onpleasant getting on with women sometimes. But, as I manages business, I generally avoids ’em. Now, what if you get the girl off for a day, or a week; then the thing’s done quietly,—all over before she comes home. Your wife might get her ear-rings, or a new gown, to make up with her.”

“I’m afraid not.”

“Lor bless ye, yes! These critters an’t like white folks; they gets over things, only manage right. Now, they say this kind o’ trade is hardening; but I never found it so. Fact is, I never could do things up the way some fellers manage. I’ve seen ’em pull a woman’s child out of her arms and set him up to sell, she screechin’ like mad;—very bad policy—damages the article. I knew a real handsome gal once, in Orleans, as was entirely ruined by this sort o’ handling. The fellow that was trading for her didn’t want her baby; and she was one of your real high sort, when her blood was up. I tell you, she squeezed up her child in her arms, and talked, and went on real awful. It kinder makes my blood run cold to think on’t; and when they carried off the child, and locked her up, she jest went ravin’ mad, and died in a week. Clear waste of a thousand dollars, just for want of management. It’s always best to do the humane thing, sir; that’s been my experience.” And the trader leaned back with virtuous decision, apparently considering himself a second Wilberforce.

With diffident zeal, he proceeded: “I believe I’m reckoned to bring in about the finest droves of niggers that is brought in,—at least, I’ve been told so; if I have once, I reckon I have a hundred times,—all in good case,—fat and likely, and I lose as few as any man in the business. And I lays it all to my management, sir; and humanity, sir, I may say, is the great pillar of my management. I’ve stuck to ’em, and realized well on ’em; yes, sir, they have paid their passage, I may say,” and the trader laughed at his joke. There was something so piquant and original in these elucidations of humanity, that Mr. Shelby could not help laughing in company. Perhaps you laugh too, dear reader; humanity comes out in strange forms now-a-days, and there is no end to the odd things humane people will say and do. Mr. Shelby’s laugh encouraged the trader to proceed.

“It’s strange,” Haley ran on, “I never could beat this into folks’ heads. There was Tom Loker, down in Natchez; a clever fellow—Tom was—only the very devil with niggers,—on principle ’t was, you see, for a better hearted feller never broke bread; ’t was his _system_, sir. I used to talk to Tom. ‘Why, Tom,’ says I, ‘when your gals takes on and cry, what’s the use o’ crackin’ on ’em? It’s natur’; and if natur can’t blow off one way, it will another. Besides,’ says I, ‘it jest spiles your gals; they get sickly, and sometimes ugly,—particular yallow gals; and it’s the devil and all gettin’ on ’em broke in. Why can’t you kinder coax ’em up, and speak ’em fair? Depend on it, Tom, a little humanity, thrown in along, goes a heap further than all your jawin’ and crackin’; and it pays better.’ But Tom couldn’t get the hang on ’t; and he spiled so many, I had to break off with him.”

“And you find your way does better?” said Mr. Shelby.

“Why, yes. When I can, I takes a leetle care about the onpleasant parts,—like selling young uns,—get the gals out o’ the way; out of sight, out of mind; and when it’s clean done, they naturally gets used to it. ’Tan’t, you know, as if ’t was white folks, brought up ’spectin’ to keep their children and wives. Niggers, fetched up properly, ha’n’t no kind o’ ’spectations; so it comes easier.”

“I’m afraid mine are not properly brought up,” said Mr. Shelby.

“S’pose not; you Kentucky folks spile your niggers. You mean well, but ’tan’t real kindness. What’s the use givin’ on ’em notions and expectations, when they’re to be hacked and tumbled round the world? Rough and tumble comes all the harder arter. Every man thinks well of his own ways; and I think I treat niggers just about as well as it’s worth while to treat ’em.”

“It’s a happy thing to be satisfied,” said Mr. Shelby, with a slight shrug.

After a pause, Haley rose. “I’m in a devil of a hurry. I shall want to know, as soon as possible, what I may depend on.”

“Well,—call up this evening, between six and seven, and you shall have my answer,” said Mr. Shelby.

“I’d like to have been able to kick the fellow down the steps,” thought Shelby, as the door closed, “with his impudent assurance; but he knows how much he has me at advantage. If anybody had ever said to me that I should sell Tom down south to one of those rascally traders, I should have said, ‘Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this thing?’ And now it must come, for aught I see. And Eliza’s child, too!—So much for being in debt,—heigho! The fellow sees his advantage, and means to push it.”

Perhaps the mildest form of slavery is seen in Kentucky. Quiet agricultural pursuits, not calling for those periodic hurries of more southern districts, make the negro’s task more reasonable; the master, content with gradual acquisition, has not temptations to that hardheartedness which sudden gain so easily buys at the price of the helpless. One who visits some estates there, and witnesses the good-humored indulgence of certain masters and the affectionate loyalty of certain slaves, might dream the patriarchal legend over again. But over all broods a portentous shadow—the shadow of law. So long as law counts these beings, with beating hearts and living affections, only as things belonging to a master,—so long as the failure, imprudence, or death of the kindest owner may any day exchange kind protection for hopeless misery and toil,—so long it is impossible to make anything beautiful or desirable in the best regulated administration of slavery.

Mr. Shelby, a fair average man, good-natured and kindly, had never stinted the physical comfort of his negroes; but he had speculated largely and loosely; involved himself deeply; and his notes to a large amount had come into Haley’s hands. This small piece of information is the key to the preceding conversation.

It so happened that, in approaching the door, Eliza had caught enough to know that a trader was making offers to her master for somebody. She thought she heard an offer for her boy; her heart swelled; she strained him so tight that the little fellow stared.

“Eliza, girl, what ails you today?” said her mistress, when Eliza had upset the wash-pitcher, knocked down the workstand, and, abstracted, offered a long nightgown instead of the silk dress ordered.

“O, missis!” cried Eliza, bursting into tears; “there’s been a trader talking with master in the parlor! I heard him.”

“Well, silly child, suppose there has.”

“O, missis, do you suppose mas’r would sell my Harry?” And she threw herself into a chair, sobbing convulsively.

“Sell him! No, you foolish girl! You know your master never deals with those southern traders, and never means to sell any of his servants, as long as they behave well. Who do you think would want to buy your Harry? Do you think all the world are set on him as you are, you goosie? Come, cheer up, and hook my dress. There, now, put my back hair up in that pretty braid; and don’t go listening at doors any more.”

“Well, but, missis, you never would give your consent—to—to—”

“Nonsense, child! to be sure, I shouldn’t. I would as soon have one of my own children sold.”

Reassured by her mistress’ confident tone, Eliza went nimbly on with the toilet, laughing at her own fears.

Mrs. Shelby was a woman of high class, intellectually and morally; to the magnanimity common to Kentucky women she added religious sensibility and principle, carried with energy into practical results. Her husband, making no particular profession, yet reverenced the consistency of hers, stood a little in awe of her opinion, and gave her unbounded scope in benevolent efforts for the comfort and improvement of her servants; in fact, he really seemed somehow or other to fancy that his wife had piety and benevolence enough for two—to indulge a shadowy expectation of getting into heaven through her superabundance of qualities to which he made no particular pretension.

The heaviest load on his mind, after the trader’s visit, lay in the foreseen necessity of breaking to his wife the arrangement contemplated,—meeting the importunities and opposition he knew he should encounter. She, ignorant of his embarrassments, and trusting his general kindliness, had met Eliza’s fears with sincere incredulity; and, being occupied with preparations for an evening visit, dismissed the matter from her thoughts.
